note.text: An incorporated company has a legal identity distinct from its owners. In the limited-liability company forms studied, owners’ ordinary responsibility for company debts is generally limited to their agreed contributions, subject to applicable rules and separate obligations such as guarantees. Shares represent ownership interests; the company’s property is not each shareholder’s personal property. Continuity can extend beyond a particular owner’s departure. A company may have a single owner where the legal form allows it, so counting owners alone does not establish the form.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to distinguish a company from its owners and calculate nominal issued share capital. Builds on: ownership and liability in sole proprietorships and partnerships. Leads to: company governance and the mix of equity and borrowing.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: An imaginary Douala processing company raises equity by issuing shares. A shareholder owns an interest, not a right to take a company vehicle home. The business may continue when an owner sells an interest under the applicable rules. All values in this exercise are nominal classroom amounts, not quoted market prices or legal minimum capital.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Separate company, shareholder and manager. Multiply the issued share count by nominal value to find nominal issued capital. Keep nominal value distinct from market price and the company’s total asset value. Limited liability is not a promise that a shareholder cannot lose an investment.

questions.prompt: A fictional company issues {n} shares with nominal value {v} CFA francs per share. What is the nominal issued share capital?

misconceptions.explain: Adding a share count to a currency value does not give capital.
That is the value per share, not the value of all issued shares.

solution: Nominal issued share capital = shares issued × nominal value.
